data.title: Psoriasis — viva
data.summary: Papulosquamous & erythroderma · 23 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Psoriasis** (Papulosquamous & erythroderma)_

**Q1. Define psoriasis.**
- Chronic, immune-mediated, genetically determined, inflammatory multisystem disease with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales, nail and joint involvement, and metabolic/cardiovascular comorbidity; relapsing–remitting course

**Q2. Epidemiology.**
- Worldwide 2–3%; India 0.44–2.8%; men slightly more in India
- Bimodal onset: type I (<40 years, HLA-Cw6/C*06:02, family history, severe) and type II (>40 years, sporadic)

**Q3. Describe the genetics.**
- Polygenic; PSORS1 on chromosome 6p21 (HLA-C*06:02 — strongest), other loci: IL23R, IL12B, TNFAIP3, CARD14 (PSORS2), IL36RN (GPP), LCE3B/C deletion, ERAP1
- Concordance ~70% in monozygotic vs ~20% in dizygotic twins

**Q4. Explain the immunopathogenesis.**
- Triggers (trauma, infection, drugs) → keratinocyte stress releases LL-37 (cathelicidin) + self-DNA/RNA → activates plasmacytoid dendritic cells (IFN-α) → myeloid dendritic cells produce IL-23 and IL-12 → Th17 and Tc17 cells produce IL-17A/F, IL-22 → keratinocyte hyperproliferation, antimicrobial peptides, chemokines (CXCL1/8 → neutrophils) — self-amplifying loop
- TNF-α (from DCs, macrophages, T cells) amplifies; IL-36 important in pustular psoriasis
- Basis for targeted therapy: TNF, IL-12/23 p40, IL-23 p19, IL-17A/F/RA, IL-36R, PDE4, TYK2

**Q5. How is epidermal cell kinetics deranged in psoriasis? (PYQ)**
- Keratinocyte cell cycle shortens from ~311 h to ~36 h; epidermal turnover time from ~28 days to 3–5 days; germinative cell population doubled with all cells cycling (growth fraction ~100% vs 60%)
- Result: immature retained-nuclei cells (parakeratosis), thin/absent granular layer, acanthosis

**Q6. Name the trigger (aggravating) factors.**
- Physical trauma (Koebner), streptococcal throat infection (guttate), HIV (severe), stress, smoking, alcohol, obesity, cold dry weather, hypocalcaemia (pustular)
- Drugs: lithium, β-blockers, antimalarials (chloroquine/HCQ), NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, interferons, terbinafine, imiquimod, TNF inhibitors (paradoxical), sudden withdrawal of systemic steroids (pustular flare), checkpoint inhibitors

**Q7. Classify psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Plaque (vulgaris, ~90%): chronic stable plaque, small/large plaque, rupioid, ostraceous, elephantine, annular
- Guttate (children/young adults after strep throat)
- Inverse/flexural (no scales, glazed), sebopsoriasis, scalp, palmoplantar (non-pustular), nail, genital
- Pustular: generalised (von Zumbusch, annular, exanthematic, impetigo herpetiformis of pregnancy, juvenile), localised (palmoplantar pustulosis, acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau)
- Erythrodermic
- Psoriatic arthritis
- Special: linear, napkin, drug-induced, HIV-associated

**Q8. Describe clinical signs in a plaque.**
- Well-demarcated, erythematous, indurated plaques with loose silvery-white micaceous scales on extensors (elbows, knees), scalp, lumbosacral area, umbilicus, natal cleft; symmetrical
- Grattage test (Auspitz sign): candle-grease sign (scraping produces more silvery scales), Burkley's membrane (thin moist glistening membrane after removal), then Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding from tips of dilated papillary capillaries due to thin suprapapillary plate)
- Woronoff's ring (pale halo around healing plaques, PG inhibition — after UV/steroids), Koebner phenomenon (lesions at sites of trauma in 7–14 days)

**Q9. Describe isomorphic (Koebner) response (PYQ).**
- Appearance of lesions of an existing dermatosis at sites of trauma (scratch, surgery, tattoo, burn, injection) — true Koebner (psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo); pseudo-Koebner by autoinoculation (warts, molluscum); reverse Koebner (lesion clears at trauma site); Wolf's isotopic response (new different disease at site of a healed one — e.g. after zoster)
- All-or-none phenomenon; occurs in 25% of psoriatics; positive Koebner suggests unstable disease

**Q10. Describe nail changes in psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Matrix involvement: pits (commonest — coarse, irregular), leukonychia, red spots in lunula, crumbling, transverse ridges (Beau's lines)
- Nail bed: oil-drop/salmon patch, onycholysis with erythematous border, subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter haemorrhages
- Nail psoriasis is common (up to 50%; 80–90% in PsA) and strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis (DIP joints)
- Assessed by NAPSI (Nail Psoriasis Severity Index, 0–8 per nail)
- Treatment: intralesional triamcinolone (matrix), topical calcipotriol-steroid, tazarotene; systemic — methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, apremilast, biologics (IL-17, TNF best)

**Q11. Histopathology of psoriasis.**
- Confluent parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum), spongiform pustules of Kogoj (neutrophils in spinous layer — pustular), hypogranulosis, regular (psoriasiform) acanthosis with club-shaped rete ridges, thinning of suprapapillary plates, dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae, perivascular lymphocytes

**Q12. Comorbidities associated with psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Psoriatic arthritis (~20–30%)
- Metabolic syndrome: obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease
- Cardiovascular disease — severe psoriasis is an independent risk factor for MI and stroke (shorter life by ~5 years)
- Crohn's disease, uveitis, depression/anxiety, alcohol use, smoking, lymphoma (CTCL), chronic kidney disease, OSA
- Screen: BMI, BP, blood sugar, lipid profile, LFT, joint symptoms (PEST questionnaire), mood

**Q13. What is psoriatic arthritis? Give CASPAR criteria.**
- Seronegative spondyloarthropathy; patterns (Moll and Wright): asymmetric oligoarthritis (commonest), DIP-predominant, symmetric polyarthritis, arthritis mutilans (telescoping fingers), spondylitis/sacroiliitis; plus enthesitis, dactylitis
- CASPAR: inflammatory articular disease + ≥3 points from — current psoriasis (2) or personal/family history (1), nail dystrophy (1), negative RF (1), dactylitis (1), juxta-articular new bone formation on X-ray (1)
- X-ray: pencil-in-cup deformity, erosions with new bone formation

**Q14. How do you assess severity?**
- PASI (Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, 0–72): erythema, induration, scaling (0–4) × area (0–6) in head (0.1), upper limbs (0.2), trunk (0.3), lower limbs (0.4)
- BSA (hand = 1%), PGA, DLQI; rule of tens — BSA >10% or PASI >10 or DLQI >10 = moderate–severe
- Treatment goals: PASI 75/90/100 response; PASI 90 now standard target with biologics

**Q15. Discuss the management of stable plaque psoriasis (PYQ).**
- Limited (<10% BSA): topical therapy — emollients, keratolytics (salicylic acid 3–6%), topical steroids (potent for body, mild for face/flexures), vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol, calcitriol) and fixed combination with betamethasone (gel/foam), coal tar, dithranol (short-contact), tazarotene, tacrolimus for face/flexures, roflumilast cream, tapinarof
- Moderate–severe or special sites/failure: phototherapy — NB-UVB 311 nm (2–3 times weekly, 20–30 sessions), PUVA (oral 8-MOP + UVA), targeted excimer laser 308 nm
- Systemic conventional: methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin, apremilast
- Biologics and small molecules for those who fail/cannot take conventional drugs (or PsA)
- General: weight loss, stop smoking/alcohol, treat comorbidities, counsel chronicity

**Q16. Methotrexate — mechanism, dose, monitoring.**
- Folate antagonist (dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor) — antiproliferative and immunomodulatory (adenosine release)
- Dose: 7.5–25 mg once weekly (oral/SC) after test dose 2.5–5 mg; folic acid 5 mg/day except methotrexate day
- Baseline: CBC, LFT, RFT, viral markers (HBV, HCV, HIV), chest X-ray, pregnancy test; monitor CBC/LFT every 2–4 weeks initially then 2–3 monthly; liver fibrosis assessment — FibroScan, PIIINP, rather than routine biopsy
- Adverse effects: bone marrow suppression (pancytopenia — risk with renal failure, NSAIDs, cotrimoxazole), hepatotoxicity/fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis/pneumonitis, mucositis, teratogenicity (stop 3 months before conception both sexes), nausea; antidote — folinic acid (leucovorin)

**Q17. Cyclosporine and acitretin key points.**
- Cyclosporine: calcineurin inhibitor (blocks IL-2 transcription in T cells); 2.5–5 mg/kg/day; fastest acting conventional drug — for erythrodermic/unstable/pregnancy-short-term; side effects: nephrotoxicity, hypertension, hypertrichosis, gingival hyperplasia, hyperlipidaemia, drug interactions (CYP3A4), malignancy; limit to 1 year, monitor BP and creatinine (reduce if >25% rise)
- Acitretin: retinoid (RAR agonist) — normalises keratinisation; 0.3–0.5 mg/kg/day (25–50 mg); best for pustular, palmoplantar, erythrodermic and in HIV; combine with phototherapy (Re-PUVA); not immunosuppressive; teratogenic — avoid pregnancy for 3 years after stopping (alcohol converts to etretinate); side effects: cheilitis, xerosis, hair loss, hyperlipidaemia, hepatotoxicity, DISH

**Q18. Discuss the role of biologics (PYQ).**
- TNF-α inhibitors: etanercept (fusion protein), infliximab (chimeric IV), adalimumab (human; biosimilars in India), certolizumab pegol (no Fc, minimal placental transfer — pregnancy)
- IL-12/23 p40: ustekinumab
- IL-17: secukinumab, ixekizumab (IL-17A), brodalumab (IL-17RA), bimekizumab (IL-17A and F)
- IL-23 p19: guselkumab, risankizumab, tildrakizumab — high efficacy with 8–12 weekly dosing
- Anti-CD6: itolizumab (Indian)
- IL-36R: spesolimab (generalised pustular psoriasis flares)
- Screening: TB (IGRA/Mantoux + CXR — TB reactivation esp. with TNF), HBV, HCV, HIV, CBC, LFT; avoid live vaccines
- Specific cautions: TNF — demyelination, heart failure (NYHA III/IV), lupus-like, paradoxical psoriasis; IL-17 — inflammatory bowel disease, Candida infections; IL-23 — very safe profile

**Q19. Oral small molecules.**
- Apremilast — PDE4 inhibitor (raises cAMP, reduces TNF/IL-23/IL-17) 30 mg BD after titration; no lab monitoring; side effects — diarrhoea, nausea, headache, weight loss, depression
- Deucravacitinib — allosteric TYK2 inhibitor 6 mg once daily; acne, URTI, raised CPK
- Oral JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib) mainly for PsA

**Q20. Discuss recent advances in management (PYQ).**
- IL-23 and IL-17A/F biologics with PASI 90–100 in most patients; biosimilars reduce cost (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, ustekinumab)
- TYK2 inhibitor (deucravacitinib), oral IL-23R peptide (icotrokinra, in development/approval)
- Topical: tapinarof (aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist), roflumilast cream/foam (PDE4), calcipotriol-betamethasone foam/cream (PAD technology)
- Spesolimab and imsidolimab for GPP
- Treat-to-target approach, early aggressive therapy to modify comorbidity risk

**Q21. Generalised pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch) — features and management.**
- Sudden fever, malaise, sheets of sterile pustules on painful erythema, lakes of pus; leucocytosis, hypocalcaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, raised liver enzymes; risk of sepsis, ARDS
- Triggers: steroid withdrawal, pregnancy, infection, hypocalcaemia, drugs; IL36RN, CARD14, AP1S3 mutations
- Treatment: admit, supportive care; acitretin (drug of choice in adults, not in women of child-bearing potential), cyclosporine (rapid), methotrexate, infliximab, spesolimab (IV, rapid pustule clearance); impetigo herpetiformis — cyclosporine/prednisolone, early delivery if severe

**Q22. Psoriasis in pregnancy and children — what treatments?**
- Pregnancy: emollients, topical steroids, NB-UVB (first choice for extensive), cyclosporine if severe, certolizumab; avoid methotrexate, acitretin, PUVA, tazarotene
- Children: topical agents, NB-UVB, methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin (short-term), etanercept, adalimumab, ustekinumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab approved in children

**Q23. Differential diagnosis of psoriasis plaque.**
- Lichen simplex chronicus, nummular eczema, seborrhoeic dermatitis (scalp), tinea corporis (KOH), pityriasis rosea (guttate), PRP, lichen planus hypertrophic, mycosis fungoides, secondary syphilis (palms/soles), Bowen's disease (single), DLE, reactive arthritis (keratoderma blennorrhagicum)

## Quick spotter facts
- Grattage: candle-grease → Burkley's membrane → Auspitz sign
- Munro microabscess, spongiform pustule of Kogoj
- Nail pits + oil-drop sign + DIP arthritis

## Note
Biologic approvals and Indian availability change often — confirm before quoting newer agents (icotrokinra, imsidolimab).

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Psoriasis); Indian psoriasis guidelines (IADVL); AAD-NPF 2019–2020 guidelines. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
